newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo Nikkei closes at highest since mid-December.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo Nikkei closes at highest since mid-December.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market returned from a long holiday weekend in a bullish mood, boosting the benchmark index above the closely watched 20,000 point barrier for the first time since mid-December.
Brokers said a buying binge by foreign investors combined with pension fund purchases to fuel a hefty gain of over three percent.
The 225-share Nikkei average surged 666.17 points or 3.41 percent higher to finish at 20,180.92, the highest closing level since 20,413.46 set on December 17.
The rise was the second largest in the calendar year, following a rise of about 815 points recorded on January 13.
June Nikkei futures were up 660 points at 20,190.

"Rounds of buying in issues which were far behind the popular blue chips, such as some financials and domestic-demand sensitive shares, in addition to bellwether issues, powered the market higher," Noboru Yorita, general manager at Tachibana Securities Co Ltd, said.

Turnover ballooned to 715 million shares, the third largest volume so far this year. On Friday, 487 million shares changed hands. Winners swamped losers 1,092 issues to 91, while 78 issues were unchanged.
Brokers said that Wall Street's rally to a record high on Monday gave the Tokyo stock market its initial confidence to continue an ascent that started last week.

The rise in the technology-oriented Nasdaq index especially inspired foreign investors to seek electricals and high-tech issues, such as Hitachi Ltd and Fujitsu Ltd, which were seen as having room to rise, they said.
A total of 276 issues, including Hitachi and Fujitsu, finished at new highs for the year, market sources said.

Hitachi was up 70 yen at 1,300 with 15.84 million shares changing hands, making it the most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo bourse. Fujitsu followed with turnover of 12.10 million shares, adding 30 yen to 1,400.

Steelmakers led by Nippon Steel Corp also climbed as investors speculated that the recent weakness of the yen against the dollar would prompt producers of basic materials to raise product prices, which would in turn boost their profits. Nippon Steel added 12 yen to 387.
The giant steelmaker was the most heavily traded issue with volume of 23.06 million shares. NKK Corp gained 11 yen to 286 while Kawasaki Steel Corp rose five yen to 387.

With the Nikkei average above the 20,000 line, following a surge of more than eight percent during a holiday-riddled week, the market is beginning to wonder how much further the Nikkei average can rise, brokers said.

"Demand from institutional investors at the start of the new fiscal year, and massive short-covering by dealers who used margin trades to meet that heavy demand, helped the index bolt higher," a fund manager at a big life insurer said.
"But participants are limited and there are few incentives to lead the Nikkei average higher. The upside is beginning to feel a bit heavy," he added.
Brokers said that private investors had little to do with the recent upswing, as the issues pumping up the indices were large issues beyond their reach.

"The recent rise has been sharp but not really overheated, partly because cash stocks have been at the centre of trade with few private investors willing to trade on margins, which would add to the volatility," said a broker at a second-tier brokerage.
In sectors, warehouses, fisheries, insurance, iron/steel and mining were at the top of the list of gainers. There were no major declining sectors.

Other indices also strengthened, with TOPIX up 41.60 points or 2.83 percent at 1,509.13. The Nikkei 300 rose 8.41 points or 2.95 percent to end at 293.64. The second section index added 24.77 points or 1.47 percent to close at 1,710.64. Turnover was 11.83 million shares against 8.68 million on Friday. The over-the-counter index stood at 1,169.44, up 20.40 points or 1.78 percent, in late Tokyo trade.
--Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk (+81-3-3432-9052)
